passage:
Dear Arohi didi,
You asked why my face was so blank at the school prize day. Honestly, I was so happy about my art prize that I was scared I'd cry in front of everyone, so I made my face stone. Last week when Riya laughed at my drawing, I did the same, to hide that it hurt. It works: nobody sees anything. But then nobody asks either, and sometimes I want them to. At home I'm not sure how to switch it off. Could you ask me a question once in a while, when we're on the terrace, and not push? I think I'd answer you.
Love, Hansa

qa.q: What prize did Hansa win?
qa.a: Hansa won an art prize.

qa.q: Why did Hansa keep a blank face on prize day and last week?
qa.a: Hansa wanted to avoid showing too much joy or hurt in front of others, which protects privacy though it also hides what Hansa needs.

qa.q: What does Hansa ask Arohi didi to do?
qa.a: Hansa asks Arohi didi for a question once in a while on the terrace, without pushing, as a chance to talk.

qa.q: How might Arohi see a blank face like Hansa's?
qa.a: She might not know whether Hansa is happy or hurt, so she may need to offer chances to talk instead of trying to read it.

grounding: A teen keeps a blank face to avoid showing hurt or joy to peers, which protects privacy but can hide need.

passage: Dilnaz, you asked how I became the girl who never reacts. It started in the hostel. First year, some girls laughed at my accent, and I noticed that when I looked upset, they laughed more. So I practised: no frown, no smile, nothing. By the second week I was good at it. Zeenat the statue, that's what they called me. It kept me safe. The problem is that I did the same when I got selected for the debate team, and no one knew I was thrilled. My roommate Sana finally put a cup of chai on my desk and said, "You don't have to show me anything. I'm just here if you want to say." I did, a week later.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat start keeping a blank face in the hostel?
qa.a: Some girls laughed at her accent and laughed more when she looked upset, so she learned to show nothing.

qa.q: What might Zeenat have been feeling when she was selected for the debate team?
qa.a: She felt thrilled, but her blank face hid it, so nobody knew.

qa.q: What did Sana do that helped Zeenat open up?
qa.a: Sana put chai on the desk and offered to listen without demanding anything, giving Zeenat a chance to talk when ready.

qa.q: How might Sana have felt about Zeenat's blank face?
qa.a: Sana may have felt unsure whether Zeenat needed help, which is why Sana waited and offered quietly instead of insisting.

grounding: A teen keeps a blank face to avoid showing hurt or joy, protecting privacy but hiding need until someone offers a chance to talk.

passage:
I'm Hrithik, and I was standing next to Sharmila when the drama club cast list went up. She'd auditioned for the lead. The lead went to someone else. Sharmila got "Villager 3."
Everyone around us was squealing or groaning. Sharmila just looked at the list. Her face was completely blank. No frown, no sigh.
"Cool," she said. "Villagers are fun."
I honestly couldn't tell what she felt. Maybe she didn't care. Maybe she did.
At lunch she was her normal self, joking. But she didn't eat her paratha.
After school I walked with her to the gate. I didn't ask about the list in front of anyone. I just said, "If you ever want to talk about the audition, I'm around. Or not. Either's fine."
She kept walking. Then, at the gate: "I practised every night for a month." Her voice cracked a little.
"I know," I said. "I heard you through the wall."

qa.q: What role did Sharmila get?
qa.a: Sharmila got "Villager 3."

qa.q: What might Sharmila have been feeling behind her blank face?
qa.a: Sharmila was probably hurt and disappointed after practising for a month, but kept a blank face to protect her privacy in front of peers.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do that offered Sharmila a chance to talk?
qa.a: Hrithik waited until they were away from others and offered to listen without pressure, saying either choice was fine.

qa.q: How might the other students have read Sharmila's reaction?
qa.a: They might have thought she didn't care about the lead, since her face and words showed nothing.

grounding: A friend's account shows a teenager keeping an impassive face to hide hurt, and a trusted friend offering a chance to talk.

passage:
Monday: In the canteen queue, a boy said loudly, "Yusuf's father sells vegetables from a cart, no?" A few laughed. Yusuf's face didn't change. He paid for his samosa and walked off. Damini, behind him, couldn't read him at all.
Wednesday: The same boy said it again in class. Yusuf stared straight ahead, blank as a wall. But Damini saw his hand gripping his pen so hard his knuckles went pale.
Thursday: After school, Damini caught up with him at the bus stop. She didn't mention the boy. She said, "My chacha has a cart near the station. Best guavas in town." Then: "If you ever want to talk about stuff, I'm around."
Friday: Yusuf sat next to her on the bus. After two stops he said, "It's not the cart. My father's proud of it. It's them laughing."
"I know," Damini said. "It's rubbish. Want to tell Ma'am together?"
He nodded.

qa.q: What does Damini's chacha have near the station?
qa.a: A cart near the station, with the best guavas in town.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling behind his blank face on Wednesday?
qa.a: Yusuf was hurt and angry, which showed only in his knuckles going pale around the pen while his face stayed impassive.

qa.q: What made Damini's approach helpful?
qa.a: She didn't push or mention the boy; she offered warmth and a chance to talk, and then suggested telling the teacher together.

qa.q: How might the boy who mocked Yusuf read Yusuf's blank face?
qa.a: He might think the jokes weren't hurting, since Yusuf's face showed nothing.

grounding: The four beats show a teenager keeping an impassive face to hide hurt, and a trusted friend offering chances to talk.

passage:
Ojas, you're wondering why your friend didn't smile when he won? Let your Chinmay Ajoba tell you about the day I kept my face like a stone.
I was fifteen. The headmaster read the scholarship results at assembly. My name was there. My elder brother's wasn't. He'd tried for two years.
I felt like shouting with joy. But he was standing three rows behind me. So I kept my face completely still. No smile. When friends congratulated me, I just nodded.
That night, I couldn't sleep. I was so happy and felt so guilty for being happy.
My grandmother noticed I'd been silent all evening. She called me to the verandah. "Chinmay, your face has been shut all day. Is it joy or sadness you're hiding?"
I said, "Both." And I finally let it out.
She held my hand and said, "You can be happy and kind at the same time."

qa.q: How long had Chinmay's elder brother tried for the scholarship?
qa.a: He'd tried for two years.

qa.q: What feelings was Chinmay hiding behind his still face?
qa.a: He was hiding joy about winning the scholarship, mixed with guilt because his brother hadn't won.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chinmay Ajoba's story?
qa.a: His grandmother noticing his shut face and calling him to the verandah to ask gently, which let him share both feelings.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's brother have felt at the assembly?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and hurt after two years of trying, which is why Chinmay hid his joy.

grounding: The elder's story shows a teenager keeping an impassive face to hide joy and guilt, and a trusted person offering a chance to talk.

passage: The school bus was packed and deafening, forty kids and a broken window rattling, when the drama teacher's message landed in the class group: the cast list for the annual play. Everyone crowded round phones. "Charu, you're not Portia! Nikita got it!" someone yelled over the noise. Heads turned to see her face. Charu kept it perfectly still. She shrugged one shoulder, said, "Cool," and went back to looking out at the traffic. Only Irawati, squashed beside her, noticed her thumbnail pressing a crescent into her palm. Irawati said nothing on the bus; there was no quiet corner in that noise and too many ears. At the stop, as the others ran off, she fell into step with Charu. "I've got nowhere to be for an hour," she said. "Samosa? You can talk or not talk." They walked two blocks before Charu said, very quietly, "I practised that speech for a month." Then her face finally moved.

qa.q: Who got the part of Portia?
qa.a: Nikita got it.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling behind the still face?
qa.a: Charu was most likely hurt and disappointed, as the thumbnail pressing into the palm hints, but hid it on the crowded bus; there may also have been pride in not showing it.

qa.q: How did Irawati offer a chance to talk?
qa.a: Irawati waited for quiet and privacy, then offered time and a samosa with no pressure: 'You can talk or not talk.'

qa.q: How might the others on the bus have read Charu's shrug?
qa.a: They probably thought Charu didn't care much, since the face stayed still and the answer was just 'Cool'.

grounding: It shows a teenager keeping a blank face to hide disappointment from peers, and a trusted person offering a private chance to talk.
